questions.title: How can a court dismiss a copyright claim on fair use grounds at the Rule 12(b)(6) stage?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the procedure here. I thought fair use is an affirmative defense that usually depends on a fact-intensive balancing of the four statutory factors, so it would normally be raised later on summary judgment, not on a motion to dismiss. But this opinion says fair use can be 'so clearly established by a complaint' that dismissal is proper under Rule 12(b)(6). What exactly has to be apparent from the complaint and incorporated materials for a court to resolve fair use this early? Is the appellate court effectively treating the videos and TV segments as documents that can be compared directly at the pleading stage?

questions.title: Why did the court say Kimmel's use was transformative even though he allegedly caused the videos to be created?
questions.question_body: The part I don't understand is Santos's argument that Kimmel 'instigated the creation' of the Cameo videos, so Kimmel was really the 'designer' of their original purpose. If Kimmel was the one who submitted the requests and got Santos to say the absurd lines, why doesn't that undermine the idea that the later TV use had a different purpose from the original work? The court seems to say the key question is what a reasonable observer would think the original videos were for, not the subjective intent of either side. Is that standard always used in transformativeness analysis, and why doesn't the alleged setup make the 'original purpose' and 'secondary purpose' the same here?

questions.title: What role does bad faith still play in fair use after Harper & Row and Warhol?
questions.question_body: The opinion says Santos argued that Kimmel's use of fake identities on Cameo showed bad faith and therefore should defeat fair use. The court responds that Harper & Row mentioned good faith, but that the Supreme Court has since 'distanced itself' from that statement. I'm having trouble understanding the modern doctrine. Does bad faith still matter under factor one, or is it basically irrelevant unless it shows an intent to usurp the copyright owner's market? If someone obtains a work through deception but then uses it for criticism or parody, how do courts now weigh that?

questions.title: Why did publication on the same day as creation matter to the second fair use factor?
questions.question_body: The court says the copyright registrations showed the videos were 'published on the same day they were created,' and it treats that as relevant to the remaining fair use factors. I'm confused about why that matters. I know the second factor looks at the nature of the copyrighted work, including whether it is unpublished, but these were still personalized expressive videos. Why does same-day publication weaken Santos's position? Is the idea that once a work has already been published, the author's interest in controlling the first public appearance is gone, even if the work is highly personal or creative?

questions.title: How did the court define market harm under factor four when the alleged use could still reduce the value of Santos's Cameo business?
questions.question_body: The opinion says there was no market harm on the face of the complaint because courts ask whether the secondary use 'usurps' the market for the original by serving as a competing substitute, not whether it just damages the original through parody or criticism. But if Kimmel's segments made Santos look ridiculous and thereby reduced demand for future Cameo videos, isn't that a real economic harm? Why is that not the kind of market harm copyright law cares about under factor four? Is the distinction that copyright protects substitution-based market injury, but not reputational or criticism-based injury?

questions.title: Why did the court avoid the Copyright Act preemption issue and instead reject the state-law claims on the merits?
questions.question_body: On the state-law claims, the district court apparently held that the contract-based claims were preempted by the Copyright Act, but the Second Circuit says it 'need not resolve this issue' because the claims fail anyway under state law. Is that a common move for appellate courts? Also, on the direct contract claim, the court says Santos was not a party to the Cameo Terms of Service and was not an intended third-party beneficiary under Illinois law. On the implied-contract claim, it switches to New York law and says there were no sufficiently pleaded essential terms or meeting of the minds. Why were different states' laws governing those two contract theories, and what would Santos have needed to allege to survive dismissal on either theory?

questions.title: Why wasn't Santos's fraudulent inducement claim enough if he was tricked into making the videos?
questions.question_body: The fraud claim is where I'm most lost. The court says Santos failed to allege any 'actual out-of-pocket loss' as required by New York law. But if he only made the videos because Kimmel misrepresented who he was and how the videos would be used, isn't that a concrete injury? Santos gave his labor, time, and performance in exchange for a transaction he says was procured by fraud. Why doesn't that count as pecuniary loss? Is this because New York fraud damages are limited to direct financial loss actually caused by the misrepresentation, and not things like benefit-of-the-bargain, reputational injury, or downstream harm from publication?
